The '''53rd Academy Awards''' ceremony, organized by the [[Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences]] (AMPAS), honored [[1980 in film|films released in 1980]] and took place on March 31, 1981, at the [[Dorothy Chandler Pavilion]] in Los Angeles, beginning at 7:00&nbsp;p.m. [[Pacific Time Zone|PST]] / 10:00&nbsp;p.m. [[Eastern Time Zone|EST]]. The ceremony was scheduled to take place originally on the previous day but was postponed due to the [[Attempted assassination of Ronald Reagan|attempted assassination]] of [[Ronald Reagan]].<ref>{{harvnb|Wiley|Bona|1996|p=592}}</ref> During the ceremony, AMPAS presented [[Academy Awards]] (commonly referred to as Oscars) in 20 categories. The ceremony, televised in the United States by [[American Broadcasting Company|ABC]], was produced by [[Norman Jewison]] and directed by [[Marty Pasetta]].<ref>{{harvnb|Osborne|2013|p=413}}</ref> Comedian and talk show host [[Johnny Carson]] hosted the show for the third consecutive time. Two weeks earlier, in a ceremony held at [[The Beverly Hilton]] in [[Beverly Hills, California]], on March 15, the [[Academy Scientific and Technical Awards]] were presented by hosts [[Ed Asner]] and [[Fay Kanin]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Past Scientific & Technical Awards Ceremonies|url=http://www.oscars.org/awards/scitech/pastawards.html|access-date=July 31, 2013 |publisher=[[Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140213185729/http://www.oscars.org/awards/scitech/pastawards.html|archive-date=February 13, 2014}}</ref>

''[[Ordinary People]]'' won four awards, including [[Academy Award for Best Picture|Best Picture]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Harmetz |first1=Aljean |title=''Ordinary People'' Wins the Academy Award for Best Picture |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1981/04/01/movies/ordinary-people-wins-the-academy-award-for-best-picture.html |access-date=January 3, 2021 |work=[[The New York Times]] |url-access=limited |date=April 1, 1981 |archive-date=February 27, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220227172303/https://www.nytimes.com/1981/04/01/movies/ordinary-people-wins-the-academy-award-for-best-picture.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Other winners included ''[[Tess (1979 film)|Tess]]'' with three awards, ''[[The Empire Strikes Back]]'', ''[[Fame (1980 film)|Fame]]'', ''[[Melvin and Howard]]'', and ''[[Raging Bull]]'' with two, and ''[[Coal Miner's Daughter (film)|Coal Miner's Daughter]]'', ''[[The Dollar Bottom]]'', ''[[The Fly (1980 film)|The Fly]]'', ''[[From Mao to Mozart: Isaac Stern in China]]'', ''[[Karl Hess: Toward Liberty]]'', and ''[[Moscow Does Not Believe in Tears]]'' with one. The telecast garnered 39.9&nbsp;million viewers in the United States.

==Winners and nominees==
The nominees for the 53rd Academy Awards were announced on February 17, 1981, by Academy president [[Fay Kanin]] and actor [[William Devane]].<ref>{{cite news |title=''Ordinary People'' Expected to Top Oscar Candidates |work=[[The Modesto Bee]] |date=February 17, 1981 |page=C4}}</ref> ''[[The Elephant Man (1980 film)|The Elephant Man]]'' and ''[[Raging Bull]]'' tied for the most nominations with eight each.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Harmetz |first1=Aljean |title=''Elephant Man'' and ''Bull'' Up for 8 Oscars Each |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1981/02/18/movies/elephant-man-and-bull-up-for-8-oscars-each.html |access-date=February 3, 2021 |work=The New York Times |url-access=limited |date=February 18, 1981 |archive-date=March 8, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210308175543/https://www.nytimes.com/1981/02/18/movies/elephant-man-and-bull-up-for-8-oscars-each.html |url-status=live }}</ref>  The winners were announced at the awards ceremony on March 31. Best Director winner [[Robert Redford]] became the third individual to win this category for his directing debut and the first actor to achieve this feat.<ref>{{harvnb|Holden|1993|p=328}}</ref> At age 20, Best Supporting Actor winner [[Timothy Hutton]] was the youngest male acting winner in Oscar history.<ref>{{harvnb|Kinn|Piazza|2002|p=226}}</ref> ''[[Fame (1980 film)|Fame]]'' became the first film to earn two nominations for Best Original Song.<ref>{{harvnb|Sackett|1995|p=248}}</ref>

==Ceremony information==
[[File:Johnny Carson 1970.JPG|thumb|left|alt=Johnny Carson in 1970|[[Johnny Carson]] hosted the 53rd Academy Awards.]]
In December 1980, the Academy hired film producer [[Norman Jewison]] to produce the telecast for the first time. "I am delighted that the Academy will have the benefit of Norman Jewison's insight and creativity," said AMPAS President [[Fay Kanin]] in a press release announcing the selection. "He has always been able to bring a fresh approach into his work."<ref>{{cite web |title=Norman Jewison to Produce 53rd Oscar Show |url=https://digitalcollections.oscars.org/digital/collection/p15759coll9/id/7394/rec/7 |publisher=Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences |access-date=June 5, 2020 |date=December 1, 1980 |archive-date=June 15, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220615081359/https://digitalcollections.oscars.org/digital/collection/p15759coll9/id/7394/rec/7 |url-status=live }}</ref> That same month, it was announced that comedian and ''[[The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson|The Tonight Show]]'' host [[Johnny Carson]] would preside over emceeing duties for the 1981 ceremony. Jewison explained the decision to hire Carson, saying that the host was "an entertainment institution whose spontaneous wit and charm would add a great deal to the quality of the show."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Saltzman |first1=Barbara |url=https://latimes.newspapers.com/newspage/387277486/ |title=Johnny, Norman, Marty, and Oscar |access-date=April 10, 2026 |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=December 27, 1980 |page=43}}{{subscription required}}</ref>

Originally, the gala was scheduled to take place on March 30. However, due to the [[Attempted assassination of Ronald Reagan|attempted assassination]] on US president [[Ronald Reagan]] which occurred earlier that day, Kanin, Jewison, and executives from broadcaster [[American Broadcasting Company|ABC]] announced that the festivities would be postponed to the following day.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Lindsey |first1=Robert |title=Academy Awards Postponed to Tonight |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1981/03/31/arts/academy-awards-postponed-to-tonight.html |access-date=March 25, 2021 |work=The New York Times |url-access=limited |date=March 31, 1981 |archive-date=November 16, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201116212356/https://www.nytimes.com/1981/03/31/arts/academy-awards-postponed-to-tonight.html |url-status=live }}</ref> It marked the first time since the [[40th Academy Awards|40th ceremony]] held in 1968 that the ceremony was postponed from its original date.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Pollock |first1=Dale |title=Backstage at Oscars, Some Hard Decisions |work=Los Angeles Times |date=March 31, 1981 |page=28}}</ref> Furthermore, producers debated whether or not to televise a pre-recorded speech from Reagan, who was a former actor,  saluting the nominees and the Academy. The segment, which was filmed nearly four weeks prior to the show, was eventually broadcast, with host Carson giving a preface explaining the decision to postpone the event.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Thomas |first1=Bob |title=''Ordinary People'' Wins |work=[[The Spokesman-Review]] |date=April 1, 1981 |page=A3}}</ref>

===''The Fly'' acceptance speech===
During the presentation of the award for Best Animated Short Film to ''[[The Fly (1980 film)|The Fly]]'', presenters [[Alan Arkin]] and [[Margot Kidder]] announced that the film's director, [[Ferenc Rofusz]] was unable to attend the ceremony. Just as they announced the Academy would accept the award on his behalf, an unnamed man later identified as Hungarofilm general manager Istvan Dosai came up on stage and accepted the award in lieu of the absent filmmaker.<ref name="Ferenc">{{cite news |url=https://latimes.newspapers.com/newspage/387158917/ |title='Mystery Man' of Oscars Identified |access-date=April 10, 2026 |work=Los Angeles Times |date=April 1, 1981 |page=7}}{{subscription required}}</ref> Marble Arch Films publicist Regina Gruss, who was in charge of hosting the Hungarian delegation at the Oscars, said that Rofusz contacted Dosai to accept the award on his behalf, but Academy officials asked him not to come up onstage unless his name was announced.<ref>{{cite news |title='Mystery Man' Had Approval |work=[[Sioux City Journal]] |date=April 2, 1981 |page=A22}}</ref> After speaking to reporters and posing for pictures backstage, he never returned to his seat and left the ceremony immediately.<ref name="Ferenc"/> According to Academy security chief Jerry Moon, AMPAS contacted the [[Los Angeles Police Department|LAPD]] to issue a search warrant for Dosai for theft. However, Academy spokesperson Art Sarno denied that the organization had contacted the police and said that Dosai returned the statuette during a post-awards banquet.<ref name="Dosai">{{cite news |title=It Was a Stand-In, Not a Phony, at Oscarcast |work=[[San Francisco Examiner]] |date=April 2, 1981 |page=A19}}</ref>

===Critical reviews===
Some media outlets received the broadcast critically. Television columnist [[Tom Shales]] of ''[[The Washington Post]]'' commented, "Everything seemed an anticlimax to the Reagan opening, and the tragic events in Washington a day earlier did put a shadow of gloom over an affair that had promised to be grim enough anyway – since all but one of the year's Best Picture nominees were somber, austere films, and nothing to shout about."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Shales |first1=Tom |title=The Oscars |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1981/04/01/the-oscars/0cb2adf8-299b-4c48-a481-da1ee3f90a13/ |access-date=September 21, 2020 |newspaper=The Washington Post |date=April 1, 1981 |archive-date=August 27, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170827130149/https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/1981/04/01/the-oscars/0cb2adf8-299b-4c48-a481-da1ee3f90a13/ |url-status=live }}</ref> ''[[The Salt Lake Tribune]]'' television critic [[Harold Schindler]] wrote, "On the whole, the 53rd annual Academy Awards telecast Tuesday was overly long, expectedly dull and surprisingly lacking in those highlights which make Oscar night conversation."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Schindler |first1=Harold |title=TV Today: Oscar Show Lacked Usual Highlights |work=[[The Salt Lake Tribune]] |date=April 2, 1981 |page=G11}}</ref> Bill Mandel of the ''[[San Francisco Examiner]]'' quipped, "After the real and completely unscripted emotional explosions of Monday, all the manipulated thrills of the movie industry seemed like the efforts of those bullfight clowns who distract the bull when the matador is injured."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Mandel |first1=Bill |title=The Big Broadcast of '81 |work=San Francisco Examiner |date=April 1, 1981 |page=E2}}</ref>

Other media outlets received the broadcast more positively. ''[[St. Petersberg Times|Tampa Bay Times]]'' film critic Robert Alan Ross remarked, "The one-day delay turned out well. President Reagan's taped greeting – combined with emcee Johnny Carson's assurance that the First Couple were comfortably watching – instilled a happier mood than might otherwise have prevailed."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Ross |first1=Robert Alan |title=Academy Award Voters Reacted to Reality |work=[[Tampa Bay Times|St. Petersburg Times]] |date=April 3, 1981 |page= 3D}}</ref> Jerry Buck of the [[Associated Press]] quipped, "Producer Norman Jewison effectively chose to make the night a homage to motion pictures' past, making wide use of many cherished film clips that tugged at the heart and memory."<ref>{{cite news |last1=Buck |first1=Jerry |title=Despite Assaination Attempt, Usual Pomp Accompanies Academy Awards |work=[[Santa Cruz Sentinel]] |date=April 1, 1981 |page=11}}</ref> ''[[The Boston Globe]]'' columnist Bruce McCabe wrote, "Given the trauma of the past few days, the Academy Awards show conducted itself rather well. No one really disgraced himself. There were no political speeches."<ref>{{cite news |last1=McCabe |first1=Bruce |title=The Celluloid Rite of Spring |work=[[The Boston Globe]] |date=April 2, 1981 |page=34}}</ref>

===Ratings and reception===
The American telecast on ABC drew in an average of 39.9&nbsp;million people over the length of the entire ceremony, which was a 19% decrease from the [[52nd Academy Awards|previous year's ceremony]].<ref>{{cite news |last1=Abramowitz |first1=Rachel |title=Oscar's Choice |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2006-jan-06-et-stewart6-story.html |access-date=February 3, 2021 |work=[[Los Angeles Times]] |date=January 6, 2006 |archive-date=June 1, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220601110557/https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2006-jan-06-et-stewart6-story.html |url-status=live }}</ref> An estimated 75&nbsp;million total viewers watched all or part of the awards.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Harris |first1=Harry |title=Original ''Saturday Night'' Crew to be on Ch. 48 Reruns |work=[[The Philadelphia Inquirer]] |date=April 3, 1981 |page=16-C}}</ref> Moreover, the show drew lower [[Nielsen ratings]] compared to the previous ceremony, with 31% of households watching over a 58% share.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Boyer |first1=Peter |title=Oscar Show's Ratings are the Third Lowest |work=[[The Pantagraph]] |date=April 7, 1981 |page=B5}}</ref> Nevertheless, the ceremony presentation won an award for Outstanding Art Direction for a Variety Program ([[Roy Christopher]]) at the [[33rd Primetime Emmy Awards|33rd Primetime Emmy]]s in September 1981.<ref>{{cite web |title=The 53rd Annual Academy Awards–Emmy Awards, Nominations and Wins |url=https://www.emmys.com/shows/53rd-annual-academy-awards |publisher=Academy of Television Arts and Sciences |access-date=November 14, 2020 |archive-date=October 20, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201020094623/https://www.emmys.com/shows/53rd-annual-academy-awards |url-status=live }}</ref>
